extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; general readers interested in press history
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and extract evaluative principles and practices for 19th-century American newspapers as described in a history of journalism. Emphasizes the roles, business models, editorial styles, and political relationships of newspapers of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of freedom of speech and of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and newspapers should assert and defend the right of freedom of speech and of the press when threatened by political authorities or mobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Charles Hammond strongly rebuked fellow editors and citizens and 're-asserted the right of freedom of speech and of the press,' declaring that attempts to molest a paper would be striking at fundamental American institutions. Anti-pattern: failing to defend controversial publishers leads to intimidation, mob action, and suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish primary hostile demands in full (transparency of source material)
rubrics_metrics.description: When political bodies or officials demand censorship or custody of editors, newspapers should print the demands in full to expose threats to press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Every time that a southern governor or southern legislature passed a bill demanding that the northern states muzzle the press or deliver some abolitionist editor... Birney printed the demand in full.' This is presented as a tactic to show the North the extent of the threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose facts demonstrating threats to civil institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should set forth factual evidence showing how institutions (e.g., free speech, free press, union of states) are being undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Birney's paper 'set forth facts that showed that free speech and the free press were threatened by those in political control of the south' — a model of journalism that uses documentation and reporting to reveal systemic threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial defense and inter-paper solidarity against mob violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials and fellow papers have a duty to rebuke calls for violence and to defend the right of editors to publish unpopular views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Though Birney was abused and threatened with lynching, Hammond's public rebuke helped temporarily protect Birney. Anti-pattern: papers that join in abuse or suggest violence facilitate suppression of press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of semi-official/administration organs to guide public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments and political leaders may create or back semi-official newspapers to inform the public and guide desirable trains of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hamilton conceived such publications; Jefferson and Jackson established or supported partisan organs (e.g., Jackson's Globe) to express administration views. Scoring note: these organs can be effective but risk becoming patronage vehicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of patronage and degeneration of 'official organs'
rubrics_metrics.description: When newspapers become administration organs, their role can degenerate into the distribution of patronage and they may lose independent influence as molders of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes the selection of official papers became 'a mere designation of so much patronage' and Jackson's patronage lessened the organ's influence. Anti-pattern: treating editorial organs chiefly as patronage positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim reporting and official stenography for Congressional debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate, verbatim reporting of legislative debates (by trained stenographers) is a valuable journalistic function and preserves historical record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gales and Seaton were the first official reporters of Congress and produced notes of the Missouri Compromise debates and other major oratorical clashes; later the Congressional Globe and the Congressional Record continued this role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from political dictation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors should maintain independence and resist being directed or taking 'dictation' from political leaders, even presidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original reporting via resident correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers increase influence by sending or keeping their own correspondents to report important events (e.g., Congressional debates) rather than relying on papers printed in the capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From 1824 onward papers began 'sending their own representatives to report [debates], relying less on the papers printed in Washington.' Noted correspondents include James Gordon Bennett and others whose independent reporting made them influential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to demand for 'uncolored' news
rubrics_metrics.description: For long-term standing, newspapers must supply uncolored (straight) news responsive to public demand, not only partisan color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: semi-official papers were 'obliged, in the long run, to be responsive to the demand for uncolored news or else to forfeit not only its standing but its existence.' Guidance: balancing interpretation with factual reporting is necessary for survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penny-press audience study and human-interest focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular/penny papers must 'study the public' and include material that interests working-class readers — details from police courts, the human side of city life, and local curiosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The penny paper 'was obliged to study the public' and found that 'what interested the penny public did not interest the six-cent public.' Success came from satisfying this demand with 'newspapers of character' and attention to facts (or fiction) about ordinary people's lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability: advertisements over raw circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper's financial success depends more on its ability to command advertising than on sheer circulation numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'the advertisements, rather than the circulation, were the means of making them profitable investments.' Practical guidance: build readership that attracts advertisers; circulation matters primarily as a means to secure adverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal journalism as an identifiable style (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common journalistic style of the era was a 'personal journalism' marked by coarse appeals to popular passions, personal attacks, and intrusion into private life — seen as crude but symptomatic of democratic change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Tocqueville's critique: American journalists 'habitually abandon the principles of political science to assail the characters of individuals, to track them into private life.' The book frames this as an inevitable surface manifestation of social change; as a cautionary anti-pattern for professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price accessibility as a means to democratize information
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering news at a price within the means of 'every one' (e.g., the penny paper) is presented as important for diffusing useful knowledge among the laboring classes and promoting democratic participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sun's stated objective: 'to lay before the public, at a price within the means of every one, all the news of the day.' Day claimed the penny press 'diffusing useful knowledge... is effecting the march of independence' among the operative classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papers must satisfy the popular curiosity for local facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful popular papers tapped 'the great curiosity on the part of the public for facts — or fiction — about their very interesting selves' and offered content accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: include local anecdotes, lively reporting, and human-centered stories; those papers that 'satisfied it with newspapers of character' survived, others did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper influence depends on urban/local centers, not solely capital organs
rubrics_metrics.description: As the country grew, the papers in large and local cities, with able editors and writers, were better positioned to affect public opinion than semi-official capital organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'it was not the organ at the capital that was most effective; the newspapers in the large cities... were the ones that were in a position to affect the public.' Practical implication: publishers should cultivate strong local/regional presence and independent talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing laws and government contract procedures affect press patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in how government printing contracts were awarded (e.g., in 1846 awarding to lowest bidder) and where laws were printed influenced the flow of patronage and the status of official newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prior practice printed laws in many state papers; later directives limited appearance to principal papers and, after 1846, contracts went to lowest bidder. This procedural standard shaped which papers benefited from government business.
